intro: Level 7 moves first and plays black; Level 8 plays red. The graph has a line for each level: its own estimate of Level 7’s winning chances at every position. Grades use Level 8’s. A flip’s grade compares it with the average over every piece still face down; the die shows whether the piece that turned up was a lucky draw.

comments.1: The opening flip turns up a black cannon on b2, so Level 7 plays black and Level 8 plays red. Averaged over every piece still face down, this flip was worth 48.1% for Level 7; the cannon gives 44.0%. The gap is the luck of the draw, not a poor choice of square.
comments.5: The black cannon on b2 jumps the face-down piece on b3 to take the red advisor on b4. A cannon needs exactly one piece to jump, and that piece can stay face down, so neither player learns what it is.
comments.10: The red elephant on a4 takes that cannon on b4. In Banqi an elephant outranks a cannon. Level 8 recaptures with a piece already face up instead of spending a turn on a flip.
comments.45: The flip on g4 turns up the red general, one of Level 8’s pieces. It still helps Level 7 here: the average flip was worth 34.2% for Level 7, and this one gives 44.8%. An opponent’s piece can be a lucky draw when it turns up in a bad place.
comments.53: The black general moves from d4 to c4. The analysis prefers d4 to e4: after the move played, Level 7’s chances fall from 96.2% to 64.5%. The side line shows that move, which needs no flip.
comments.57: The black soldier on h4 could take the red general on g4. Level 7 passes up this capture for several moves; after moving the black elephant from c1 to b1 instead, its chances fall from 63.6% to 57.5%.
comments.58: The red soldier on c4 takes the black general on b4. This is Banqi’s one exception to rank: a soldier can take a general, so the strongest piece still has to watch the weakest.
comments.206: The red advisor moves from b3 to b4 and takes the last black soldier. Level 7 has no legal move left, which loses in Banqi, so Level 8 wins.
